newsitem.title: VIETNAM: FEATURE-British firm trailblazes wine on Vietnam minefields.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE-British firm trailblazes wine on Vietnam minefields.

text.p: British businessman Tony Allen likes challenges. As a manager at the first joint venture winery in Vietnam it appears he's got one.

"Initially when I saw what was here I thought it couldn't be done," he says. "But these are early days and the conditions here are better than in China, which produces thousands of bottles each year."

The Allied Domecq Ninh Thuan Co Ltd winery, situated just outside this dusty southern coastal town, is very much a venture in the spirit of a British winegrowing tradition of battling against the odds, and sometimes also, the critics.
The $3 million plant, a venture between Allied Domecq and the local People's Committee a day's drive north of Ho Chi Minh City, is a long way from anywhere.

On one side is what, until last year, was a forgotten minefield. Nearby lies wartime scrap. Perhaps more significantly, it's set beneath a blazing tropical sun less than 12 degrees north of the equator.
"We were quite upset when a local magazine said our wine tasted like cola," says Allen. "If you look at the wine that's been available here, it's fair to say this is far superior."

Allen is being no apologist. The plant, which began producing sweet reds, whites and a sparkling white at the beginning of this year, is aimed initially at pleasing not foreign, but Vietnamese palates more used to Russian "champagne" -- a relic of Vietnam's former Soviet links.
The technology is Australian, so is the expertise that's been used to turn local workers into trained wine technicians.
"The Shiraz and Sauvignon blanc seem to be doing quite well so far," says technical manager Huynh Thanh Loc as he points to experimental vines growing in a former minefield beside the plant.
"The grapes are growing very fast, from cuttings to vines in just a few months."
The problem of finding the right grape is probably the most immediate one for a winery anywhere in the world. At present surrounding farms produce only the sweet Red Cardinal eating variety.
But, inevitably in Vietnam's difficult, shifting and still-nascent business environment, a venture of this nature faces a range of sometimes unexpected difficulties.

"Not many people have corkscrews in Vietnam," says Trevor Shoppee of Allied Domecq's Ho Chi Minh City office. "They open a wine bottle by using a chopstick, so we're having to think about replacing the corks with screw-cap tops."
Bigger troubles, however, afflict marketing and distribution for a product aimed at Vietnam's domestic market of 77 million people, whose per capita earnings are less than $300 per year.
By unhappy coincidence the government announced a total ban on cigarette and alcohol advertising -- except for beer -- just days after the winery produced its first bottles.
Finding reliable outlets for produce is also not easy when shops are mostly tiny street-side vendors.
In addition, sales promotions in Vietnam, where the communist authorities are seeking to stamp out luxuriant consumerism, can also be notoriously difficult to get approved.
And then there are the occasional differences of opinion with the local partners.
"Vietnamese people would like it more if the label said 'champagne' instead of 'sparkling wine'," says production manager Bui Tat Vu. Allen frowns.

Company executives skirt details both of how they'll overcome these obstacles and their longer-term ambitions for the plant. Wine consumption in Vietnam barely registers against a beer-drinking rate of around 750 million litres a year.
Allied Domecq, also a drinks distributor in Vietnam, says simply that the aim is to achieve "satisfactory results" within three years.

But, if successful, the hope is that vineyards will be established inland from here in the cooler central highlands, where the grapes necessary for a quality wine that can be exported should in theory be more easily attainable.
"It will come right, you have to hang on there," says Allen. "It's a very small market. We've got to sell this on quality and recognition."
